title: The end of the Cow
hookLine: the messenger believes, and the prayer not to be burdened (2:284–286)
tomorrow: Dadi drags Amira out to the yard at night. what is she looking at?

cards: The thud of a backpack hitting the floor at the end of a long day. Amira's has three textbooks in it, finals start Monday, Dadi's knee exercises run every evening, and Hana still isn't really talking to her.
She drops the bag in the hallway and sits on the stairs. Dadi, passing with her tea, says four words in English and keeps walking: "Not beyond its scope."
They come from the last lines of al-Baqarah, the Cow, and they were sent down to people who were sitting on the floor too.

teach.b: Here is the story, from Sahih Muslim. A verse came near the end of al-Baqarah saying Allah will bring people to account for what is in their minds, shown or hidden.
The companions came to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and dropped to their knees. This, they said, is more than we can bear.

He told them not to answer as some before them had, we hear and we disobey, but to say, in Pickthall's words: "We hear, and we obey." They said it. They kept saying it until their tongues were used to it.

And then the last two verses came. The first describes them: the messenger believes, and the believers, in Allah, His angels, His scriptures and His messengers, "We make no distinction between any of His messengers."
The second answers the weight: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope."

teach.h: IF WE FORGET, OR MISS THE MARK.
teach.b: Then the verse turns into a prayer the Qur'an itself gives: "Our Lord! Condemn us not if we forget, or miss the mark!"
Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: the relief came after they said we hear and obey, not before. And the Prophet said that whoever recites these two verses at night, they are enough for him.

how: Muslims recite the last two verses of al-Baqarah at night, often after the night prayer or in bed, following the hadith that they suffice whoever recites them.

games.q: what does “the end of the cow” mean?
o: the chapter where the Qur'an tells a cow's story
the final verse revealed before the Prophet died
the last verses of al-Baqarah, recited at night

games.q: how the weight was answered — tap the pairs.
p: on their knees: too much to bear
say: we hear, and we obey

s: 'not beyond its scope' means a believer never feels overwhelmed
the companions felt crushed and said so, on their knees. the verse came to them there.
a hadith says the last two verses of al-Baqarah, recited at night, are enough
whoever recites them at night, they suffice him (Sahih al-Bukhari).

games.q: you're among the companions. a verse says even your hidden thoughts will be accounted for. it feels unbearable. what does the Prophet tell you to say?
o: this is beyond us; ask Allah to take it back.
nothing yet; wait and see what comes next.
games.why: they said it until it came easily, and then the last two verses came: 'Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope.'

practice: Pull something with real weight onto your lap: a bag, a stack of books, a heavy blanket. Feel exactly how much it is for a few breaths, then set it down beside you and feel your legs without it.
Stay with the lighter feeling for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: The end of the Cow: the last two verses of al-Baqarah, recited at night, where a crushing verse is answered with not beyond its scope.

orig.note: Arabic: we hear, and we obey, the companions' answer in 2:285.

carryVoice: The line for the night: we hear and obey, and then the weight is measured to the soul. Three passages in.
